title: Express & APIs
intro: Most Node backend jobs involve building HTTP APIs, usually with Express or Fastify. Interviewers use these questions to see if you understand what the framework actually does with a request: middleware order, how errors travel, what changed in Express 5, and how to make an API behave predictably with correct status codes, validation, limits and logs. A senior answer explains the mechanism and then the production gotcha.

questions.title: How middleware works
questions.question: How does Express middleware work? What does next() do, why does order matter, and how is app.use different from app.get?
questions.short: Express keeps one ordered list of layers. For each request it walks that list top to bottom and runs every layer whose method and path match. Each layer gets (req, res, next): it either ends the response, or calls next() to pass control to the next matching layer, or calls next(err) to jump to error handlers. app.use matches any method and any path that starts with the prefix; app.get matches only GET on that exact route pattern.
questions.simple: Middleware is like an assembly line. Each worker can do a bit of work and pass the item on, or take it off the line and ship it right away.

explain.p: Every `app.use`, `app.get`, `router.post` and so on adds a layer to an ordered stack. When a request comes in, Express starts at the top and checks each layer: does the path match, and (for route handlers) does the method match? If yes, it calls the function. The function decides what happens next.

list: Call `next()` to hand control to the next matching layer.
Send a response (`res.json`, `res.send`, `res.end`) and do not call `next()` — this is called short-circuiting. Later layers never run.
Call `next(err)` to skip all normal layers and go to the next error-handling middleware (the ones with 4 arguments).
Call `next('route')` inside a route handler to skip the remaining handlers of that route only.

explain.note: If a layer does none of these — no response and no next() — the request just hangs until the client or a proxy times out. This is a classic bug.

explain.p: Because the list is walked top to bottom, a layer only affects the layers that come after it. Body parsers must come before the routes that read `req.body`. Auth must come before the routes it protects. The 404 handler must come after all routes, and the error handler must be last.

explain.caption: A typical, deliberate ordering

explain.note: Middleware can also be scoped: `app.get('/admin', requireAdmin, handler)` runs `requireAdmin` only for that route. Prefer this over global middleware with `if (req.path === ...)` checks.

anim.title: A request walks the middleware stack

steps.note: The app has six layers in this exact order. Express will walk them from the top for every request.
A GET arrives. requestId runs first, adds an id to req, then calls next().
express.json() only parses when Content-Type is JSON. A GET has no body, so it just calls next().
auth checks for an Authorization header. It is there, so the if-block is skipped.
auth calls next(). Control moves to the next layer that matches GET /users/42.
The route matches. getUser loads the user and calls res.json(). The response is now sent.
getUser did not call next(), so notFound and errorHandler never run for this request. The walk is over.
A second request arrives with no token. requestId and json() pass it along as before.
auth sends 401 and returns without calling next(). This is short-circuiting: the route handler is never reached.
Takeaway: each layer either ends the response or calls next(). Order decides who gets to run first.

followups.q: What happens if middleware calls next() and then also sends a response?
followups.a: Both paths run. A later layer may also send a response and you get "Cannot set headers after they are sent". Use `return next()` or `return res.json(...)` so only one path continues.

followups.q: What does next('route') do?
followups.a: It skips the remaining callbacks of the current route (for example the handler after a check) and continues with the next matching route. It only works in app.METHOD/router.METHOD handlers, not in app.use.

followups.q: Is middleware run for static files too?
followups.a: Yes, express.static is just a middleware. Put it before expensive middleware like auth or body parsing if static files are public, so they are served without that cost.

mistakes: Forgetting to call next() or send a response, which leaves the request hanging.
Registering the body parser after the routes, so req.body is undefined.
Thinking app.use("/api") matches only exactly "/api" — it matches every path under it.
Calling next() and then continuing to run code that writes to res.

questions.title: Router and modular routes
questions.question: How do you split a growing Express app into modules? How does express.Router work?
questions.short: express.Router() creates a mini-app with its own middleware stack and routes. You build one router per resource in its own file and mount it with app.use('/api/orders', ordersRouter). Inside the router paths are relative to the mount point. Router-level middleware only runs for requests that reach that router, and mergeParams: true lets a nested router read params from its parent path.
questions.simple: A router is like a department in a store. The front door sends you to the right department, and each department has its own rules inside.

explain.p: A `Router` has the same methods as `app` (`use`, `get`, `post`, `route`, `param`) but it is not a server. You mount it on a path prefix. When a request matches the prefix, Express strips the prefix and lets the router walk its own stack.
By default a child router cannot see params from the parent mount path. Pass `{ mergeParams: true }` when you create it.

list: `app.js` builds the app (middleware, routers, 404, error handler) and exports it — no `listen()`. This makes it easy to test with supertest.
`server.js` imports the app and calls `listen()`, plus graceful shutdown.
`routes/*.js` wire paths to handlers and validation.
`controllers/` or `handlers/` hold thin HTTP logic; `services/` hold business logic that knows nothing about req/res.

explain.note: Keep req/res out of your service layer. A service that takes plain arguments can be reused from a queue worker or a CLI and is much easier to unit test.

followups.q: Why export the app separately from calling listen()?
followups.a: Tests can import the app and pass it to supertest, which binds it to an ephemeral port. It also lets server.js own startup and shutdown concerns.

followups.q: What is router.param?
followups.a: router.param('orderId', fn) runs fn once per request whenever a route with :orderId matches, before the handler. It is handy for loading the resource and attaching it to req, but it can hide logic, so many teams prefer explicit middleware.

followups.q: Do routers add much overhead?
followups.a: Very little. Each mount is one extra layer to match. The bigger cost is a long list of regex routes in a single router, which still is rarely the bottleneck compared with I/O.

mistakes: Forgetting mergeParams and wondering why req.params.parentId is undefined in a nested router.
Putting business logic directly in route files so nothing can be reused or unit tested.
Calling app.listen() inside app.js, which makes tests open real ports and conflict.

questions.title: Error middleware and 404s
questions.question: How does error-handling middleware work in Express, and how do you handle 404s?
questions.short: Error-handling middleware has exactly four parameters: (err, req, res, next). Express recognises it by its arity. When anything calls next(err) or a sync handler throws, Express skips all normal middleware and jumps to the next error handler. A 404 is not an error in Express: it is just a request that no route answered, so you add a normal middleware after all routes that sends 404, and put the error handler last.
questions.simple: Normal middleware is the main road. Calling next(err) takes the emergency exit straight to the error desk, skipping every stop in between.

explain.h: How Express finds the error handler

explain.p: Express checks `fn.length`. Functions with 4 declared parameters are error handlers; everything else is normal middleware. When an error is passed to `next`, Express skips layers until it finds an error handler. When there is no error, error handlers are skipped.

explain.note: You must declare all four parameters, even if you do not use `next`. If a linter removes the unused `next`, the function has 3 params and silently becomes normal middleware.

list: Never leak stack traces or DB error text for 5xx errors. Log them, return a generic message plus a request id.
Check `res.headersSent`: if a stream already started, you cannot send JSON. Delegate to the default handler, which closes the connection.
Errors from libraries like body-parser already carry `status`/`statusCode` (for example 400 for bad JSON, 413 for a too-large body), so reading those keeps them correct.

explain.p: Without this, Express sends its built-in HTML page "Cannot GET /x". Note the difference between "no such route" (this handler) and "route exists but the record does not" (your handler calls `next(new AppError(404, ...))`).

anim.title: next(err) jumps over normal middleware

steps.note: Four layers. Only the last one has 4 parameters, so only it is an error handler.
GET /orders/999 matches the route. The handler looks up the order.
No order found. The handler calls next(err) with a NotFoundError (status 404).
Because an error is pending, Express skips auditLog. It has 3 params, so it is normal middleware.
The 404 handler has 2 params, also normal middleware, so it is skipped too.
The error handler runs. It reads err.status = 404.
It sends a JSON error. The message is shown because 4xx errors are safe to expose.
Now GET /nope arrives. No route matches, auditLog calls next(), and the 404 handler answers.
Two different 404s: "record missing" goes through next(err); "no such route" falls through to the catch-all.

followups.q: Can you have more than one error handler?
followups.a: Yes. They run in order. A common pattern is one that maps known errors (validation, DB unique violations) to 4xx and calls next(err) for the rest, then a final catch-all that logs and returns 500.

followups.q: What if the error handler itself throws?
followups.a: Express catches it and passes it to the next error handler, or to its built-in final handler, which responds with the error's status (or 500) and includes the stack trace only when NODE_ENV is not production.

followups.q: Where do you handle errors thrown outside requests?
followups.a: In process-level handlers: process.on('unhandledRejection') and process.on('uncaughtException'). Log them and shut down gracefully, because the process may be in an unknown state.

mistakes: Declaring the error handler with 3 parameters, so it never receives errors.
Registering the error handler before the routes.
Returning raw error messages or stacks for 500s, leaking internals.
Treating unmatched routes as errors and expecting the error handler to catch them.

questions.title: Async errors: Express 4 vs 5
questions.question: What happens when an async route handler throws in Express? How is Express 5 different from Express 4?
questions.short: In Express 4, a sync throw is caught and sent to the error handler, but an async handler returns a promise and Express 4 ignores it. A rejection becomes an unhandled rejection: the request hangs and, since Node 15, the process crashes by default. You must catch and call next(err), or wrap handlers. Express 5 checks the returned value: if a handler or middleware returns a promise that rejects, it calls next(err) for you.
questions.simple: Express 4 hands work to an async function and walks away without waiting to hear if it failed. Express 5 waits for the answer and reports failures to the error desk.

explain.p: Express 4 calls your handler inside a try/catch. That catches synchronous throws only. An `async` function never throws synchronously — it returns a rejected promise. Express 4 does not look at the return value, so nobody handles it.

list: The client never gets a response and waits until it times out.
Node emits `unhandledRejection`. Since Node 15 the default mode is `throw`, so the process crashes if there is no handler.
Errors from callbacks and timers (`setTimeout(() => { throw ... })`) are also not caught in either version — they happen on a different call stack.

explain.p: Express 5 (stable since late 2024) uses router 2.x. When a middleware or handler returns a promise that rejects (or throws inside an async function), the router calls `next(err)` with the rejection value. A rejection with no value is turned into an Error. So plain `async` handlers just work, and you can delete the wrappers.

explain.note: Express 5 only forwards the promise you return. If you start work and do not await it (fire-and-forget), or throw from inside a callback-style API, it still escapes. Always `await` or `return` the promise.

list: Path syntax changed (path-to-regexp v8): a bare `*` must be named, e.g. `/*splat`, and optional parts use braces like `/users{/:id}`.
`req.body` is `undefined` (not `{}`) when no body parser ran.
`req.query` is a getter, so you cannot assign to it in validation middleware.
`res.status()` only accepts valid integer status codes and throws otherwise.

anim.title: A rejected promise in Express 4 vs Express 5

steps.note: Express 4 calls the async handler. It returns a pending promise right away. Express 4 does not keep it.
The DB call fails. await throws inside the async function, so its promise rejects.
No .catch is attached. Node fires unhandledRejection. The default (Node 15+) is to crash the process.
The wrap() fix: the wrapper calls the handler and chains .catch(next) on its promise.
The DB call rejects. .catch(next) receives the error and calls next(err).
Express routes the error to the error handler, which sends a 500 JSON body.
Express 5: no wrapper. The router itself looks at the returned promise.
It rejects, so the router calls next(err). Same result as wrap(), with less code.
Rule: in Express 4 every async error must reach next(err). Express 5 does it for returned promises only.

followups.q: Does Express 5 catch errors thrown inside setTimeout or an EventEmitter callback?
followups.a: No. Those run on a different call stack and are not part of the promise the handler returned. Promisify the API or catch the error and call next(err) yourself.

followups.q: How do you migrate a big Express 4 app to 5?
followups.a: Read the migration guide, fix path patterns (named wildcards, optional braces), stop mutating req.query, check code that relied on req.body being {}, and then remove async wrappers. The official codemods help with some renames.

followups.q: Should you add a global unhandledRejection handler?
followups.a: Yes, to log and then shut down gracefully. Do not use it to keep running as if nothing happened: the request that failed is still hanging and state may be inconsistent.

mistakes: Believing Express 4 catches async errors because it catches sync throws.
Claiming Express 5 catches every async error, including those in callbacks or un-awaited promises.
Wrapping with .catch(next) but forgetting to return/await inner promises, so the wrapper sees a resolved promise.

questions.title: Request lifecycle and "headers already sent"
questions.question: What causes "Error [ERR_HTTP_HEADERS_SENT]: Cannot set headers after they are sent to the client", and how do you prevent it?
questions.short: An HTTP response has one status line and one set of headers, written once. As soon as you call res.json, res.send, res.end or write the first body chunk, the headers go out and res.headersSent becomes true. Any later attempt to set a header or status throws ERR_HTTP_HEADERS_SENT. It almost always means two code paths answered the same request: a missing return after sending, calling next() and also sending, or a callback that fires twice.
questions.simple: You can only post a letter once. Trying to change the address after it is in the mailbox does not work.

list: Before anything is sent you can freely change `res.statusCode` and headers.
`res.json()`/`res.send()` set Content-Type and Content-Length, then call `res.end()`. The status line and headers are written first, then the body.
`res.write()` sends headers on the first chunk (streaming). After that, only more body bytes or `end()` are allowed.
When the response finishes, `res` emits `finish`. If the client disconnects first, `res` emits `close` without `finish` having fired.
Use `return res.status(404).json(...)` so the function stops.
Keep one exit point per handler where you can, or use early returns consistently.
In error handlers, check `if (res.headersSent) return next(err)`.
For streams, use `stream.pipeline` (from `node:stream/promises`) so errors and completion are handled once.

explain.note: In an async handler the thrown ERR_HTTP_HEADERS_SENT becomes a rejected promise. In Express 4 that is an unhandled rejection; in Express 5 it reaches your error handler, which must not try to send again.

anim.title: Two code paths try to answer one request

steps.note: Request comes in. Nothing is sent yet, so headers and status can still change.
The DB returns null: there is no user 999.
res.status(404).json() sets status and Content-Type, then ends the response. Headers go on the wire.
There is no return, so the function keeps going past the if-block.
res.json(null) tries to set Content-Type again. Headers are already sent, so Node throws.
The client already got its 404. In Express 5 the rejection reaches the error handler (which must not send again); in Express 4 it is an unhandled rejection.
Fix: write "return res.status(404).json(...)" so only one path can send.

followups.q: How can you detect that a response has already been sent?
followups.a: Check res.headersSent. It is true once headers are written. res.writableEnded tells you end() was called.

followups.q: How do you run code after the response is finished, for example for logging duration?
followups.a: Listen for res.on('finish') for a completed response and res.on('close') to also catch aborted connections. Libraries like pino-http and on-finished do this for you.

followups.q: Can you change the status after starting a stream?
followups.a: No. Once the first chunk is written, the status and headers are fixed. If a stream fails midway, the only option is to destroy the connection so the client sees a truncated response.

mistakes: Writing res.json(...) without return inside an if-block.
Calling next() after sending a response.
Error handlers that always send, even when headers were already sent by a stream.

questions.title: Request validation
questions.question: How do you validate request input in an Express API and return consistent error responses?
questions.short: Validate every input at the edge — body, params and query — with a schema library like Zod or Joi, in a reusable middleware. On failure return 400 (or 422) with a stable, machine-readable shape: an error code, a message and per-field details. On success, pass the parsed, typed and coerced data on and use only that. The same shape should be used for every error the API returns.
questions.simple: Check everything at the front door against a checklist, and when something is wrong always fill in the same complaint form so the client knows where to look.

explain.h: Why a schema, not hand-written ifs

list: Schemas strip or reject unknown fields, which blocks mass-assignment (a client sending `role: "admin"`).
Query strings and params are always strings. A schema coerces `"20"` to `20` and enforces ranges.
With Zod you get TypeScript types from the same schema (`z.infer`), so code and validation never drift.

explain.p: Pick one shape and use it everywhere — validation, auth, not found, conflicts, 500s. A popular standard is RFC 9457 "Problem Details" (`application/problem+json` with `type`, `title`, `status`, `detail`, `instance`). Either way, clients should be able to switch on a stable `code`, not parse English messages.

explain.note: Validation is not only for security. It is also where you set limits: max string lengths, max array sizes, max page size. Unbounded inputs are a common way to make a single request very expensive.

followups.q: 400 or 422 for validation errors?
followups.a: Both are used. 400 means the request is malformed; 422 (Unprocessable Content) means it is well-formed but semantically invalid. Many APIs use 400 for schema failures and 422 for business-rule failures. What matters is being consistent and documenting it.

followups.q: Should you also validate responses?
followups.a: It can be worth it for public APIs: a response schema prevents accidentally leaking fields like passwordHash. Fastify does this natively; in Express you can serialize through a DTO or schema.

followups.q: Where should business rules like "email already taken" live?
followups.a: In the service layer, not the schema. The schema checks shape; the service checks state, and maps a unique-constraint violation to 409 Conflict.

mistakes: Validating req.body but forgetting params and query.
Passing req.body straight into an ORM create(), allowing mass assignment.
Returning a different error shape from every endpoint.
Echoing raw validation library errors that expose internal field names or stack traces.

questions.title: HTTP status codes done right
questions.question: Which HTTP status codes should an API use, and how do you choose between similar ones like 401 vs 403 or 400 vs 422?
questions.short: 2xx for success: 200 with a body, 201 for created (with a Location header), 204 for success with no body. 4xx when the client must change something: 400 malformed, 401 not authenticated, 403 authenticated but not allowed, 404 not found, 409 conflicts with current state, 422 well-formed but semantically invalid, 429 rate limited with Retry-After. 5xx when the server failed: 500 for bugs, 503 when temporarily unavailable or overloaded. The key rule: the code tells clients and proxies whether retrying could help.
questions.simple: The status code is the one-word answer before the details: OK, created, your fault, not allowed, try later.

head: Code
Meaning
Use it when
rows: GET, or PUT/PATCH that returns the resource
POST that created something. Add a Location header
DELETE, or updates that return nothing. Never send a body
Invalid JSON, wrong types, failed schema
Missing, expired or invalid credentials. Send WWW-Authenticate
User is known but lacks permission
Also to hide existence of resources the user may not see
Duplicate email, stale version in optimistic locking
Overload, maintenance, dependency down, shutting down. Retry-After helps

list: 401 vs 403: 401 says "who are you?" — logging in could fix it. 403 says "I know who you are, and the answer is no."
403 vs 404: for private resources, returning 404 avoids revealing that the resource exists.
400 vs 422: 400 for "cannot parse/shape is wrong", 422 for "I understood it but it breaks a rule". Be consistent.
409 vs 422: 409 when the conflict is with the current state of the server (someone else changed it, already exists). 422 when the payload itself is invalid regardless of state.
500 vs 503: 500 means a bug; 503 means "temporarily, try again". Load balancers and clients treat them differently.

explain.p: Clients and proxies make decisions from the code. 4xx usually means "do not retry the same request" (except 408 and 429). 5xx, especially 502/503/504, are often retried — so only return 5xx when retrying might actually help, and only for idempotent operations unless you support idempotency keys.

explain.note: Do not return 200 with { success: false }. It breaks caching, monitoring dashboards, retries and every HTTP client's error handling.

followups.q: What status do you return during graceful shutdown?
followups.a: Stop accepting new connections and let in-flight requests finish. If a request still arrives, 503 with Connection: close tells the load balancer to send it elsewhere.

followups.q: What about 202 Accepted?
followups.a: Use it when work is queued and not finished yet. Return a way to check progress, such as a Location header pointing to a status resource.

followups.q: Should a DELETE of a missing resource be 404 or 204?
followups.a: Both are defensible. 204 makes DELETE naturally idempotent from the client's view; 404 is more informative. Pick one and document it.

mistakes: Using 401 for "logged in but not allowed" (that is 403).
Returning 500 for validation failures or not-found cases.
Sending a body with 204.
Returning 200 for every response and putting the real status in the JSON.

questions.title: Idempotency, PUT vs PATCH
questions.question: Which HTTP methods are idempotent, and what is the difference between PUT and PATCH?
questions.short: Idempotent means sending the same request once or ten times leaves the server in the same state. GET, HEAD, OPTIONS, PUT and DELETE are idempotent; POST and PATCH are not guaranteed to be. PUT replaces the whole resource with the body you send, so repeating it is safe. PATCH sends partial changes; a 'set field' patch is effectively idempotent, but an 'increment' or 'append' patch is not. For POSTs that must be safe to retry, like payments, accept an Idempotency-Key header and return the stored result for repeats.
questions.simple: Pressing an elevator button five times still calls one elevator — that is idempotent. Dropping five coins in a vending machine is not.

head: Method
Safe (no state change)
Idempotent
Typical use
rows: Create or fully replace at a known URL

explain.p: Idempotency is about server state, not the response. A second DELETE can return 404 instead of 204 and still be idempotent, because the resource is gone either way.

explain.h: Why it matters in Node code

explain.p: Networks fail. A client, a proxy or your own retry logic may resend a request after a timeout even though the first one succeeded. For idempotent methods this is harmless. For POST it can create two orders or charge twice.

list: With PUT, validate the full schema; missing fields mean "remove/reset", not "keep".
With PATCH, validate a partial schema (`schema.partial()` in Zod) and update only provided keys. Decide how `null` is treated (clear the field) vs missing (keep it).
Avoid PATCH bodies that express relative operations (`{ "balanceDelta": 10 }`) unless you protect them with an idempotency key or version check.

explain.caption: Simplified: real implementations also lock the key while the first request is still running

explain.note: The check-then-save above has a race if two identical requests arrive at the same time. Insert the key first with a unique constraint (status 'in_progress'), and let the second request get a conflict.

followups.q: Is GET always safe to retry?
followups.a: It should be, as long as your GET handlers have no side effects. A GET that changes state (like /logout or /delete?id=1) breaks that contract and is also a CSRF risk.

followups.q: Can PUT be used to create?
followups.a: Yes, when the client chooses the id or URL: PUT /users/7 creates user 7 if missing (201) or replaces it (200/204). Repeating it is still idempotent.

followups.q: What is JSON Merge Patch vs JSON Patch?
followups.a: JSON Merge Patch (RFC 7396) sends a partial document where null deletes a key. JSON Patch (RFC 6902) sends a list of operations like add/remove/replace. Merge Patch is simpler and is what most APIs mean by PATCH.

mistakes: Saying idempotent means "returns the same response every time".
Treating PUT as partial update and silently keeping missing fields.
Automatically retrying POST requests on timeout without idempotency keys.

questions.title: Pagination: offset vs cursor
questions.question: How would you paginate a list endpoint? Compare offset and cursor pagination.
questions.short: Offset pagination (?page=3 or ?offset=40&limit=20) is simple and supports jumping to any page, but the database still reads and throws away all skipped rows, so deep pages get slow, and inserts or deletes between requests cause duplicates or skipped items. Cursor (keyset) pagination sends an opaque cursor from the last item and queries WHERE (sort_key) < cursor ORDER BY sort_key LIMIT n. It uses an index, is fast at any depth and stable under writes, but cannot jump to page N. Always cap the limit and sort by a unique, indexed key.
questions.simple: Offset is like saying "skip the first 500 books" — you still have to count them. A cursor is a bookmark: you open right where you left off.

explain.code: SELECT id, total FROM orders ORDER BY id DESC LIMIT 20 OFFSET 4000;

list: Pros: trivial to build, page numbers, total counts are natural.
Cons: OFFSET 4000 still scans 4020 rows. Response time grows with depth.
Cons: if a new row is inserted at the top between page 1 and page 2, every row shifts and the client sees one item twice. A delete makes the client miss one.
The response includes `nextCursor`, an opaque token (for example base64url of the last id, or of `createdAt|id`).
The next query uses `WHERE id < :lastId` — an index range scan, the same cost on page 1 or page 1000.
Fetch `limit + 1` rows to know if there is another page without a COUNT query.
If you sort by a non-unique column like `created_at`, add a tie-breaker: `WHERE (created_at, id) < ($1, $2) ORDER BY created_at DESC, id DESC`, with a composite index.

explain.code:
const encode = (s) => Buffer.from(s).toString('base64url');
const decode = (s) => Buffer.from(s, 'base64url').toString();
explain.caption: Opaque cursors let you change the format later without breaking clients

explain.note: Whatever you choose, cap `limit` on the server (for example max 100). An unbounded `?limit=1000000` is an easy way to take down your API and your database.

anim.title: Cursor pagination stays correct when rows are added

steps.note: Client calls GET /orders?limit=3. Table has orders 101 to 107, newest first.
No cursor yet, so "before" is the largest safe integer: start from the newest row.
Ask for limit + 1 = 4 rows using the index on id. The 4th row tells us if more pages exist.
hasMore is true. Return 3 items and a cursor that encodes the last id, 105.
Meanwhile a new order 108 is inserted at the top. With OFFSET 3, page 2 would now start at 105 again: a duplicate.
With the cursor, page 2 asks WHERE id < 105. The new row does not shift anything.
Page 2 is 104, 103, 102 with nextCursor enc(102). No duplicates, no gaps.
Page 3 fetches WHERE id < 102: only 101 comes back, fewer than limit + 1, so hasMore is false and nextCursor is null.

followups.q: How do you support "previous page" with cursors?
followups.a: Return a prevCursor built from the first item and query in the opposite direction (id > cursor ORDER BY id ASC), then reverse the results before returning them.

followups.q: How do you return a total count cheaply?
followups.a: Often you do not. If the UI needs it, use an estimate (for example Postgres reltuples or EXPLAIN row estimates) or cache the count, because COUNT(*) on large filtered tables is expensive.

followups.q: What if the client changes filters or sort order mid-way?
followups.a: The cursor is only valid for the same filters and sort. Encode them into the cursor or reject a cursor used with different parameters.

mistakes: Not capping the limit parameter.
Using cursor pagination on a non-unique sort key without a tie-breaker, so rows with equal values are skipped.
Exposing raw DB ids or SQL in the cursor and then being unable to change it.
Sorting by a column that has no index, so even keyset pagination is slow.

questions.title: Body limits and file uploads
questions.question: How do you handle file uploads in Express, and how do you protect the server from very large request bodies?
questions.short: express.json() and express.urlencoded() buffer the whole body in memory, so they have a limit option (default 100kb) and reply 413 when it is exceeded. Files come as multipart/form-data, which those parsers ignore; use multer (built on busboy). Always set limits on file size, file count and field size. For big files, stream to disk or object storage instead of memoryStorage, so memory use stays flat. Validate type by content, not by the client's filename or mimetype.
questions.simple: Do not let strangers pour an unlimited bucket of water into your sink. Set a size limit, and for big loads, pipe it straight to the drain instead of holding it.

explain.p: When the body is too large, the parser stops reading and calls `next(err)` with `status: 413` and `type: 'entity.too.large'`. Bad JSON gives a 400 with `type: 'entity.parse.failed'`. Your error handler should map these instead of returning 500.

list: `upload.single(field)`, `upload.array(field, max)`, `upload.fields([...])` — only accept the fields you expect. Unexpected file fields give `LIMIT_UNEXPECTED_FILE`.
`dest` / `diskStorage` streams each file to disk as it arrives. `memoryStorage` keeps the whole file in a Buffer — fine for small files only.
`limits`: `fileSize`, `files`, `fields`, `fieldSize`, `parts`. Without them, a client can send an endless upload.
When a limit is hit, multer stops, removes partial files it wrote, and calls `next` with a `MulterError`.
`file.mimetype` and `file.originalname` come from the client. Check the real type by reading magic bytes (for example with the `file-type` package) and generate your own file names.
Never use `originalname` in a path: `../../etc/passwd` style names lead to path traversal.
Store uploads outside the web root, or in object storage, and scan them if users download each other's files.

explain.caption: Sketch: pipeline handles backpressure so a slow destination slows the client instead of filling RAM

explain.note: Also set server-level limits: `server.requestTimeout` (default 300000 ms since Node 18) and `server.headersTimeout`, plus a limit at the reverse proxy (for example nginx `client_max_body_size`). Defense in depth beats one setting.

anim.title: An upload streams to disk until it hits the limit

steps.note: multer is configured with a 5 MB file limit and at most 1 file.
A 3 MB avatar starts arriving. busboy parses the multipart boundaries as chunks come in.
Each chunk is written straight to a temp file. Only a small buffer is in memory at a time.
If the disk is slow, the write stream signals backpressure and reading from the socket pauses.
The file is complete. req.file has the path and size, and the handler replies 201.
Next, a client sends a 50 MB file to the same endpoint.
At 5 MB busboy reports the limit. multer stops writing and deletes the partial file.
multer calls next(err) with a MulterError. The error handler maps LIMIT_FILE_SIZE to 413.
Memory stayed small the whole time because the file was streamed, never fully buffered.

followups.q: Why not just use memoryStorage and upload the Buffer to S3?
followups.a: Memory use becomes file size times concurrent uploads. Ten 200 MB uploads at once is 2 GB of heap. Streaming keeps memory proportional to chunk size.

followups.q: What does 413 mean?
followups.a: Content Too Large (formerly Payload Too Large): the server refuses the body because it is bigger than it will accept.

followups.q: How do you let clients upload very large files without passing through Node at all?
followups.a: Give them a pre-signed URL for object storage. Node only signs the URL and later verifies the object, so the bytes never hit your server.

mistakes: Raising the global JSON limit to 50mb to make one endpoint work.
Using multer with no limits.
Trusting the client-provided mimetype or file name.
Buffering whole files in memory for large uploads.

questions.title: CORS in Express
questions.question: Your frontend on app.example.com gets a CORS error calling your API on api.example.com. What is going on and how do you configure CORS correctly in Express?
questions.short: CORS is a browser rule: a page may only read responses from another origin if that server opts in with Access-Control-Allow-Origin. For non-simple requests (PUT, DELETE, JSON content type, Authorization header) the browser first sends an OPTIONS preflight and only sends the real request if the preflight allows that origin, method and headers. In Express, use the cors middleware with an explicit origin allowlist, credentials: true only if you need cookies, and make sure it runs before auth so OPTIONS is not rejected with 401.
questions.simple: The browser asks the API: "This page from app.example.com wants to talk to you — do you allow that?" The API's headers are the answer.

explain.p: The browser does, not your server. curl, Postman and other servers ignore CORS completely. That is why CORS is not an access control mechanism for your API — it only controls which web pages can read your responses inside a user's browser.

list: Simple: GET/HEAD/POST with only basic headers and Content-Type of text/plain, multipart/form-data or application/x-www-form-urlencoded. Sent directly; the browser just checks the response headers before giving it to JS.

Preflighted: anything else — PUT/PATCH/DELETE, `Content-Type: application/json`, custom headers like Authorization. The browser sends `OPTIONS` with `Origin`, `Access-Control-Request-Method` and `Access-Control-Request-Headers` first.
Use an allowlist of origins. Reflecting any Origin back with `credentials: true` lets every website make credentialed calls and read the results.
`Access-Control-Allow-Origin: *` cannot be combined with credentials. The browser rejects it.
If the response varies by origin, the cors package adds `Vary: Origin` so caches do not serve one origin's headers to another.
`maxAge` lets the browser cache the preflight, saving a round trip on every call.
Register cors before auth and before routers, so preflight `OPTIONS` requests are answered without needing a token.

explain.note: A CORS error in the browser console is often hiding a real server error: if your 500 response comes from a handler that runs before cors, or a proxy that strips headers, the browser reports CORS instead of the 500. Check the network tab.

anim.title: Preflight, then the real request

steps.note: JS on app.example.com calls fetch PUT /api/profile with a JSON body and a Bearer token.
PUT and the Authorization header make this a non-simple request, so the browser sends a preflight first.
The cors middleware sees an allowed origin and answers the OPTIONS itself with 204. No route or auth runs.
The browser checks the answer and caches it for 600 seconds. Now it sends the real PUT.
Express runs auth and the handler. cors adds Allow-Origin to the response too.
The browser sees a matching Allow-Origin and hands the response to JS.
Now evil.example tries the same PUT. Its origin is not in the list, so the preflight gets no CORS headers.
The browser never sends the PUT. Note: for a simple GET, the request would still reach the server; only reading the response is blocked.

followups.q: Does CORS protect against CSRF?
followups.a: Not by itself. Simple cross-site requests like a form POST are still sent with cookies; CORS only stops the attacker reading the response. Use SameSite cookies and CSRF tokens for that.

followups.q: Why do I see the OPTIONS request but not the PUT?
followups.a: The preflight failed: wrong origin, missing method or header in the allow lists, or the OPTIONS request hit auth and got a 401/302.

followups.q: Is it OK to use origin: true?
followups.a: It reflects any origin. It is acceptable for a fully public, credential-less API, but with credentials: true it effectively disables the protection.

mistakes: Thinking CORS protects the API from non-browser clients.
Using a wildcard origin together with cookies or credentials.
Putting cors after the auth middleware so preflights get 401.
Fixing CORS errors by turning off web security in the browser during development and forgetting the real cause.

questions.title: Structured logging with request IDs
questions.question: How do you set up logging in a production Express API so you can trace one request across all its log lines?
questions.short: Use a structured JSON logger like pino, which is fast because it does minimal work on the main thread and writes newline-delimited JSON. Give each request an id — reuse a trusted incoming X-Request-Id or generate one — attach a child logger to req via pino-http, return the id in the response header, and include it in error responses. For code deep in services that has no req, store the logger or id in AsyncLocalStorage. Redact secrets like Authorization headers and passwords.
questions.simple: Give every request a tracking number, like a parcel. Every log line about it carries that number, so you can find its whole journey with one search.

explain.p: A JSON line like `{"level":30,"reqId":"7f3a","userId":42,"msg":"order created"}` can be filtered and aggregated by your log system. `console.log('order created for ' + id)` can only be grepped. pino is also much cheaper than console.log on the hot path, and `console.log` writes to stdout synchronously when it is a file or terminal.
pino-http logs one line per completed request with method, url, status code and response time, and sets `req.id` and `req.log`. Every line from `req.log` carries the same `reqId`.

explain.h: Request context without passing req everywhere

list: Log levels: `error` for things that need action, `warn` for handled oddities, `info` for business events, `debug` off in production.
Pretty printing (`pino-pretty`) is for development only. In production write JSON to stdout and let the platform ship it.
Propagate the id to downstream HTTP calls (`x-request-id` header) so other services log the same id.
Never log full bodies by default: they contain passwords, tokens and personal data.

explain.note: Only trust an incoming X-Request-Id if it comes from your own proxy or you validate its format. Otherwise attackers can inject giant or misleading values into your logs.

followups.q: Why is pino faster than winston or console.log?
followups.a: It does very little per call: no string formatting, fast JSON serialization, and transports (pretty printing, shipping) can run in a worker thread via pino.transport so the main thread just writes bytes.

followups.q: What is the difference between a request id and a trace id?
followups.a: A request id identifies one request in one service. A trace id (for example W3C traceparent with OpenTelemetry) follows a request across many services with parent/child spans. You can log both.

followups.q: How do you log errors properly with pino?
followups.a: Pass the error under the err key: log.error({ err }, 'msg'). pino's standard serializer then includes type, message and stack. Passing it as a string loses the stack.

mistakes: Logging Authorization headers, cookies or passwords.
Using string concatenation instead of structured fields.
Logging the whole request body on every request.
Using pino-pretty in production, which is slow and breaks log parsing.

questions.title: Express vs Fastify
questions.question: How does Fastify differ from Express, and when would you choose one over the other?
questions.short: Fastify is built around JSON Schema: route schemas validate input with Ajv and compile fast serializers for output, which also strips fields you did not declare. It has a radix-tree router, a built-in pino logger, first-class async handlers, lifecycle hooks, and an encapsulated plugin system where each plugin gets its own scope. It usually handles noticeably more requests per second on simple benchmarks. Express is simpler, has the largest ecosystem and familiarity; in real apps the database and I/O often matter more than framework overhead.
questions.simple: Express is a flexible toolbox you assemble yourself. Fastify is a toolbox with a built-in rulebook that checks and packs data for you, a bit faster.

head: Express
Fastify
rows: Built in: JSON Schema via Ajv, or type providers for TypeBox/Zod
Compiled serializer from response schema; unknown fields dropped
Native: return a value to send it, throw to error
pino built in, request id per request

explain.p: `app.register(plugin, { prefix: '/admin' })` creates a child context. Hooks, decorators and plugins registered inside it only apply there, not to siblings. To share something with the parent (like a DB connection decorator), wrap the plugin with `fastify-plugin`. This replaces the Express habit of carefully ordering global middleware.

list: Request lifecycle hooks: `onRequest` → `preParsing` → `preValidation` → `preHandler` → handler → `preSerialization` → `onSend` → `onResponse`, plus `onError`.
Express-style middleware can be used through `@fastify/middie` or `@fastify/express`, mainly for migration.
Pick Fastify for new JSON APIs where throughput, built-in validation/serialization and structure matter.
Pick Express when the team knows it well, you depend on Express-only middleware, or you are extending an existing Express codebase.
Measure your real endpoints. If each request spends 30 ms in Postgres, saving 0.1 ms in the framework will not change much.

followups.q: Why does a response schema make Fastify faster?
followups.a: fast-json-stringify generates a serializer function specialised for that shape, avoiding the generic work JSON.stringify does. It also acts as a safety filter for extra fields.

followups.q: Can you return a value and also call reply.send in Fastify?
followups.a: No. In an async handler you either return the payload or call reply.send and return reply. Doing both leads to a double-send warning and an error.

followups.q: How do you share a DB pool across Fastify plugins?
followups.a: Create a plugin that decorates the instance (fastify.decorate('db', pool)) and wrap it with fastify-plugin so the decorator is visible to the parent and its other children. Close the pool in an onClose hook.

mistakes: Claiming Fastify is faster in every real app without measuring.
Forgetting fastify-plugin and wondering why a decorator is undefined in another plugin.
Not defining response schemas in Fastify and losing both speed and field filtering.
